# Incident Report — Network Forensic Analysis

**Evidence:** `2024-08-15-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (18,189 frames, 1962.2 sec / ~33 min, capture start 2024-08-15 04:09:43 +0400). No IDS/Suricata alert export was present in the evidence directory — findings below are derived entirely from packet-level analysis with `tshark`.

## Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | 10.8.15.133 |
| MAC address | 00:1c:bf:03:54:82 (Intel NIC) |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-H8ALZBV |
| AD domain / NetBIOS | lafontainebleu.org / LAFONTAINEBLEU (DC: WIN-JEGJIX7Q9RS.lafontainebleu.org, 10.8.15.4) |
| Logged-in Windows user | **plucero** (observed as Kerberos CNameString on AS-REQ/TGS-REQ traffic originating from 10.8.15.133) |
| Browser used at infection | Microsoft Edge 127.0.2651.98 (Windows 10 x64) |

## Malware Family

**Attribution: behavioral, not signature-confirmed** (no IDS/Suricata alerts were supplied as evidence, so no rule-based/signature naming is possible).

The payload is a loader whose embedded PDB debug path identifies its internal build as:

```
E:\work\ooooooops\181\knock_v1.1.8\knock\bin64\knock.pdb
```

Behaviorally, the infection chain matches a commodity loader / initial-access malware pattern: fake-invoice lure → oversized junk-padded JScript dropper → BITS-staged native DLL → persistent HTTP beaconing to a bare-IP C2 using a deliberately archaic User-Agent and Cookie-smuggled, base64-looking encrypted payloads. I could not corroborate a specific named public malware family (e.g. via signature) from the pcap alone — treat "knock loader" (per the PDB string) as the grounded identifier and the described TTPs as the supporting behavioral evidence.

## Infection Timeline (relative to capture start 04:09:43 +0400)

| t (sec) | Event |
|---|---|
| 74.7 | Edge GET to `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?16553a25e45250a41fd5&endeds=MIGpq&JStx=59bf050d37df88a9-ade43358-eaa1220b-0571422b-0f33e6aa150e86bafd0ed4&Ld=9d7502d88d752a27b1d00587309184b5a215` → HTTP 200, `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="Invoice 876597035_003.zip"` (2,767,804 bytes) |
| ~100.2 | DNS query for `business.checkfedexexp.com` (referenced inside the delivered JS as a data-privacy link) |
| 135.9–136.2 | `Microsoft BITS/7.8` HEAD then GET of `http://72.5.43.29/data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` → 159,232-byte PE32+ x64 DLL delivered |
| 196.9 onward | Repeated GET/POST `http://72.5.43.29/` beacons with a spoofed legacy User-Agent, continuing every 5–15 sec for the remainder of the capture (last seen at t=1962.2, i.e. through capture end) |

## Indicators of Compromise

**Command-and-control**
- `72.5.43.29:80` (HTTP) — bare-IP C2, no DNS resolution observed for it. 306 GET/POST requests to `/` with User-Agent `Mozilla / 5.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1; SV1; .NET CLR 1.0.3705)` and a ~350-byte base64-style encrypted blob carried in the `Cookie:` header (e.g. `1dPYCLQThlalsevmZ8Gm4HAmczKbbrMbgfmn54P1NiJU+wBW3j6N4FgI2V+FhKDNLc2JDftSo6dUu64LJvCcj19H2UQB82SG/...`). Also used to stage the DLL payload via `HEAD`/`GET /data/0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4` (Microsoft BITS/7.8 user-agent).

**Malicious domains**
- `quote.checkfedexexp.com` (resolves to 104.21.55.70, 172.67.170.159 — Cloudflare-fronted) — delivery site for the invoice ZIP
- `business.checkfedexexp.com` (same IPs) — queried/referenced during the same session

**Malicious URL**
- `http://quote.checkfedexexp.com/managements?16553a25e45250a41fd5&endeds=MIGpq&JStx=59bf050d37df88a9-ade43358-eaa1220b-0571422b-0f33e6aa150e86bafd0ed4&Ld=9d7502d88d752a27b1d00587309184b5a215`

**Transferred files**

| File | Size | SHA256 |
|---|---|---|
| Invoice 876597035_003.zip (delivered filename) | 2,767,804 bytes | `798563fcf7600f7ef1a35996291a9dfb5f9902733404dd499e2e736ea1dc6fc5` |
| Invoice-876597035-003-8331775-8334138.js (zip contents; padded with ~7MB of unrelated scraped document text as an anti-AV/size-evasion technique — only true logic found in cleartext is a `WScript.Sleep(10000);` delay) | 6,990,020 bytes | `dab98819d1d7677a60f5d06be210d45b74ae5fd8cf0c24ec1b3766e25ce6dc2c` |
| 0f60a3e7baecf2748b1c8183ed37d1e4 (second-stage payload, PE32+ x64 DLL, internal name `knock.dll` per PDB) | 159,232 bytes | `b7aec5f73d2a6bbd8cd920edb4760e2edadc98c3a45bf4fa994d47ca9cbd02f6` (MD5 `59b7b8d29252a9128536fbd08d24375f`) |

## Notes / What Is Not Confirmed

- No filesystem/registry artifacts are visible in a packet capture, so persistence mechanism (e.g. Run key, scheduled task, Startup shortcut) could not be verified from this evidence and is **not** asserted here.
- All background Microsoft/Adobe/Akamai/Bing/MSN traffic and Windows Update BITS transfers (`msedge.b.tlu.dl.delivery.mp.microsoft.com`, `oneocsp.microsoft.com`, etc.) were reviewed and are legitimate OS/browser telemetry, not part of the incident.
- No other bare-IP or anomalous TLS SNI destinations were found beyond `72.5.43.29` and the `checkfedexexp.com` domains.
